faqs.q: We bought a list six months ago. Is it worth importing?
faqs.a: Import it, but do not let it present as new work. Freshness banding keeps an old list visibly old, so reps calibrate their expectations and you can measure connect rate by band rather than blaming effort. If the oldest band converts at a fraction of the newest, you have a purchasing decision to make, not a coaching one.

faqs.q: What is the difference between confidence and grade?
faqs.a: Grade says how good a lead is; confidence says how much we know about it. A lead with a name and a phone number and nothing else might be excellent. We simply cannot tell yet. Scoring it low would claim it is weak, which is a different and less honest statement than admitting the record is thin.

faqs.q: Does the intake check use AI?
faqs.a: No. It is deterministic arithmetic on formats and completeness, phone shape, email validity, duplicate matching, field coverage, B2B versus B2C signals. Roughly eighty per cent of understanding a dataset does not require a model, and a rule you can read is easier to trust than one you cannot.

faqs.q: Can I see why a lead's grade changed?
faqs.a: Yes. Every score change is written to an append-only timeline with the grade, confidence and all three sub-scores frozen at that moment, so a drop traces to the event that caused it, intent decay, a duplicate detection, or an ICP change that re-graded the book.

faqs.q: How is data quality different from lead qualification?
faqs.a: Qualification asks whether this buyer is worth pursuing. Data trust asks whether the record describing them is reliable enough to act on. A perfect-fit company with a mistyped phone number passes qualification and fails on data, and the fix is to correct the field rather than to disqualify the company.

title: Sales Execution Measurement
metaTitle: Measuring Sales Execution: Did the Rep Do the Thing? | Leadkaun
metaDescription: Activity dashboards measure effort, not execution. How to measure whether reps worked the right lead first, whether they followed the recommendation, and what that predicts.
h1: Sales Execution Measurement, end to end
dek: Revenue tells you what happened last quarter. Execution tells you what will happen next, but only if you measure the behaviour rather than the activity count.

quickAnswer.question: How do you measure sales execution rather than sales activity?
quickAnswer.answer: Activity metrics count what a rep did, calls made, emails sent. Execution metrics ask whether they did the right thing: was the first lead they contacted this morning one the system had ranked at the top, how fast did a high-grade lead get a response, and how many committed follow-ups were actually completed. Leadkaun measures the rank a lead held in its rep's queue at the moment of first contact, and how often a recommendation shown to a rep was accepted. It measures whether recommendations were followed, not whether they worked.

keyTakeaways: Activity counts are the easiest thing to measure and the easiest thing to game. A rep can make forty calls and work the wrong forty leads.
The most useful execution metric is positional: what rank did the lead a rep called first hold in their own queue?
Measuring adoption is not the same as measuring effectiveness. Say which one you have.
Execution data becomes surveillance the moment it is used without grade context. Tied to lead grade and outcome, it is coaching.

body.heading: Activity is not execution
paragraphs: Almost every CRM reports activity: calls logged, emails sent, meetings booked. These are easy to capture and easy to compare, which is why they persist. They are also close to useless as a predictor, because they measure volume of effort rather than allocation of it.

A rep making forty calls a day is working hard. Whether they are working the right forty leads is a separate question, and it is the one that determines the quarter. Two reps with identical activity counts can produce very different revenue, and the activity report cannot explain the gap, which is why weekly reviews built on it turn into arguments about effort.

Execution measurement asks a different question: given everything this rep could have done today, did they do the highest-value available thing? That requires knowing what the highest-value thing was, which means it only works on top of a ranking.

body.heading: The positional metric
paragraphs: The single most informative execution metric is positional. When a rep makes their first contact of the day, what rank did that lead hold in their own queue?

If it is consistently in the top few, the rep is working the ranking and the system is earning its place. If it is consistently far down, one of two things is true: either the rep does not trust the ranking, or the ranking is wrong. Both are worth knowing, and neither shows up in an activity count.

Leadkaun captures this rank at the moment of first contact and stores it on the lead. A lead contacted from within the top ten counts as working the queue. Aggregated over a fortnight it produces a straight answer to a question most teams cannot answer at all: is the prioritisation actually being used?

body.heading: Adoption versus effectiveness, say which you have
paragraphs: There are two distinct claims a vendor can make about a recommendation engine, and they are routinely conflated. The first is that reps follow the recommendations. The second is that following them produces better outcomes. The first is much easier to measure.

Leadkaun measures the first. When a recommendation is shown and a rep acts on it, that acceptance is recorded, and the ratio of accepted to shown gives an adoption rate. When a rep dismisses one, they pick a reason from a fixed list rather than typing free text, so the reasons are countable.

We do not currently compute whether the recommendation worked. The events needed to close that loop are being recorded, but no success rate is derived from them yet, and claiming otherwise would be the kind of thing this site now checks for automatically. Adoption is a real and useful number; it is not the same number as effectiveness, and a vendor that blurs them is telling you something about their evidence standards.

body.heading: Response time, measured where it matters
paragraphs: Speed to lead is the most-cited metric in sales and one of the most carelessly measured. An average across all leads is close to meaningless, because it mixes the enquiry that arrived at 3 AM with the one that arrived mid-morning, and the junk submission with the qualified buyer.

The number worth watching is response time on high-grade leads during working hours. That isolates the failure that actually costs money: a Grade A lead arriving at 10 AM and going untouched until the afternoon. Everything else is noise around that.

The corresponding daily measure is whether the team is on pace at all. Leadkaun scores execution against the shape of an Indian working day rather than a flat target, so being behind at 11 AM and being behind at 4 PM mean different things, and the manager alert fires when it still matters rather than the next morning.

body.heading: Where measurement turns into surveillance
paragraphs: Execution data is coaching material or it is surveillance, and the difference is entirely in how it is framed and what it is tied to.

The failure mode is a leaderboard of raw activity. It produces exactly the behaviour it counts: more calls, shorter calls, and quiet gaming of whatever the metric is. Reps are not being dishonest when this happens. They are responding rationally to what is being measured.

Tied to lead grade and outcome, the same data reads differently. A rep with high call volume and a six-hour response time on Grade A leads has a triage problem, not an effort problem, and telling them so is useful. That is a specific, fixable observation rather than a ranking, and it is the only version of this that survives contact with a real team.

body.heading: What to instrument first
paragraphs: Two numbers are enough to start. First, the share of Grade A leads that got a first contact on the day they arrived. Second, the queue rank of the lead each rep contacted first. Both are direct readouts of execution and both move before anything appears in closed-won.
Add follow-up completion against committed follow-ups third. It is a better predictor than total activity because it measures a promise the rep made rather than a quota someone set for them.

Resist adding more. Every additional metric dilutes attention and increases the chance that the team optimises for the wrong one. Three numbers a manager checks are worth more than a dashboard nobody opens.

faqs.q: Do you measure whether the recommendation worked?
faqs.a: No, and we will not say otherwise. We measure whether it was followed, the ratio of accepted to shown recommendations, and the queue rank of the lead a rep contacts first. The events needed to compute an effectiveness rate are being recorded but no such rate is derived yet. Adoption and effectiveness are different claims.

faqs.q: Isn't this just rep surveillance?
faqs.a: It becomes surveillance when it is an activity leaderboard, because that measures effort and invites gaming. Tied to lead grade and outcome it is diagnostic: a rep with high call volume and slow response on Grade A leads has a triage problem, which is a coachable, specific observation rather than a ranking.

faqs.q: What is the single best execution metric to start with?
faqs.a: The share of Grade A leads contacted on the day they arrived. It is unambiguous, it moves quickly, and it isolates the failure that actually costs revenue, a good lead going cold while a rep works something older.

faqs.q: Why measure the queue rank of the first contact?
faqs.a: Because it answers whether the prioritisation is being used at all. If reps consistently open leads from far down their queue, either they do not trust the ranking or the ranking is wrong, and both are worth discovering before you attribute a bad quarter to effort.

faqs.q: Does this work if reps are in the field with poor connectivity?
faqs.a: Signal logging queues locally when the connection drops and syncs on reconnect, so a call logged in a basement is not lost. That matters for the measurement as much as for the rep: execution data with systematic gaps where coverage is bad produces misleading conclusions about the reps who travel most.
